To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the use of effective interactions in empirical potentials improves their performance in discriminating between native structures and near‐native structures; 2) effective potentials contain a larger amount mutual information; 3) effective potentials filter out atom connectivity effects and 4) the shape of the effective energy function for direct interactions is almost unaffected when indirect interactions are considered.

the definition of effective interactions in knowledge‐based potentials significantly improves the performance at discriminating between the native and near‐natural conformations and that the shape of the potential energy functions is strongly influenced by the additivity assumption.

(1) the use of effective energy functions improves the performance of knowledge‐based potentials; (2) effective energy functions are less dependent on the additivity assumption than empirical energy functions; and (3) effective energy functions for indirect interactions are less dependent on direct atomic interactions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a simple procedure to obtain and use knowledge‐based potential energy functions that are more likely physically meaningful.
the development and application of knowledge‐based potentials that are based on effective interactions.
the use and the derivation of effective knowledge‐based potentials that are based on the incorporation of effective atomic interactions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, although empirical energy functions are not able to reproduce the observed effective interactions, they are able to capture some of their properties and, as a result, can be used for the discrimination between native and non‐native protein conformations.

the use of the observed effective interactions in the definition of empirical energy functions improves the ability of the energy functions to discriminate between native and near native structures, and also that the observed effective interactions are a key factor to be considered when deriving and using empirical energy functions.
effective energy functions are more robust and reliable than those derived from the observed interactions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, when deriving effective potentials, we should be careful to avoid the use of indirect atomic interactions, which are not physically relevant and are not correlated with the corresponding direct interactions.

the use of empirical energy functions that are based on effective atom interactions is an effective approach to improve the discrimination power of knowledge‐based potentials and, therefore, to improve their use for the prediction of protein structures and interactions.
effective interactions are more likely to represent physically relevant interactions, which are more likely to contribute to a mutual information content in the potential.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the definition of effective interactions in empirical energy functions is a simple procedure to obtain energy functions with better performance in discriminating between native‐like conformations and that the use of empirical potentials with effective interactions is an important step toward the use of more realistic energy functions in protein structure and protein–ligands docking.
the use of the effective energy function is a simple and straightforward procedure that can be easily implemented to improve the performance of knowledge‐based energy functions.
the use of knowledge‐based potentials can be significantly improved by the use of effective pairwise interactions.
